short: A bond whose interest payment is reset at regular intervals in line with a benchmark interest rate, instead of staying fixed for its whole life.
kid: Imagine Grandma gives you sweets every week. When the shop gives everyone more sweets, she gives you more too, and when it gives fewer, you get fewer.
detail: A floating rate bond (or floating rate note, FRN) pays a coupon equal to a reference rate plus a fixed spread, reset periodically, often every three or six months. Globally the reference is usually an overnight rate such as SOFR; in India, government FRBs have been linked to recent 182-day Treasury bill yields, and the RBI's Floating Rate Savings Bonds reset every six months at a fixed margin above the National Savings Certificate rate. Because the coupon catches up with market rates at each reset, the bond's price stays close to face value, so it carries far less interest-rate risk than a fixed-coupon bond. It still carries credit risk: if the issuer weakens, the fixed spread becomes too small and the price falls. Common confusion: a floater protects against rising interest rates, not directly against inflation.
example: Say ABC Ltd issues a ₹10 lakh floating rate bond paying the 6-month benchmark rate plus 1%, reset every six months. If the benchmark is 6.5% at a reset, the annual coupon becomes 7.5% and the next half-yearly payment is ₹37,500; if the benchmark falls to 5.5%, the payment drops to ₹32,500.
formula: Coupon rate = Reference rate + Fixed spread (quoted margin)

short: A bond whose principal, and therefore its interest payments, rise with an inflation index, so the investor's purchasing power is protected.
kid: Imagine you lend a friend a jar of marbles. If marbles get harder to find, your friend promises to give back a bigger jar, so you can still play the same games.
detail: An inflation-indexed bond adjusts its principal by a price index, such as the consumer price index (CPI), and pays a fixed real coupon on that adjusted principal. As inflation lifts the principal, each coupon and the final repayment rise too. US Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), launched in 1997, are the best-known example, and the UK has issued index-linked gilts since 1981. India issued capital indexed bonds in 1997 and inflation-indexed bonds in 2013, linked first to WPI and then to CPI in a retail version, but demand was thin and issuance stopped. The yield on these bonds is a real yield; the gap between a normal bond's yield and the linker's yield, the breakeven inflation rate, shows the market's inflation expectation. Common confusion: they protect against inflation, not against rising real interest rates, which still push their prices down.
example: Say you buy a $1,000 inflation-indexed bond with a 1% real coupon, paid once a year. If inflation over the year is 3%, the principal rises to $1,030 and the coupon is 1% of $1,030, or $10.30. A normal 1% bond would still pay $10 on $1,000.
formula: Adjusted principal = Face value × (Current index / Base index); Coupon = Real coupon rate × Adjusted principal

short: Interest earned on a bond since its last coupon date but not yet paid; the buyer pays it to the seller along with the price.
kid: If you look after a friend's puppy for three days and your sister does the rest of the week, you should get your share of the treats for your three days.
detail: Bonds pay coupons only on fixed dates, typically every six months, but the interest is earned day by day. When a bond is sold between coupon dates, the buyer will receive the full next coupon, so the buyer compensates the seller for the days the seller held it. That amount is accrued interest, calculated with the bond's day-count convention: Indian government securities use 30/360, while US Treasuries use actual/actual. Accrued interest explains why the price you pay (the dirty price) is higher than the price quoted on screen (the clean price). It matters for accounting and tax, since the seller's share is interest income, not a capital gain. Common confusion: accrued interest is not a premium or extra profit for anyone; it is simply a fair split of the coming coupon.
example: Say a bond with ₹100 face value pays a 7.2% coupon twice a year, ₹3.60 per half-year. If you buy it 60 days after the last coupon date (30/360, so 180 days per period), you pay the seller accrued interest of ₹3.60 × 60/180 = ₹1.20 per ₹100 of face value.
formula: Accrued interest = (Annual coupon / Coupons per year) × (Days since last coupon / Days in coupon period)

short: A bond's price without the interest earned since the last coupon date; it is the price usually quoted on trading screens.
kid: It's like the price tag on a toy before the shop adds the batteries you also have to pay for.
detail: The clean price is a bond's price excluding accrued interest, normally quoted per 100 of face value. Markets quote clean prices because the full price follows a saw-tooth: it climbs daily as interest accrues and then drops when the coupon is paid. Stripping that pattern out lets traders see genuine price changes caused by interest rates and credit quality. In India, government securities on NDS-OM are quoted clean, and accrued interest is added at settlement. The cash you actually pay or receive is the dirty price, which equals the clean price plus accrued interest. Common confusion: a bond quoted at 98.50 does not mean you pay only ₹98.50 per ₹100 of face value; you also pay the accrued interest, so the amount that leaves your account is larger.
example: Say a G-sec is quoted at a clean price of ₹98.50 and accrued interest is ₹1.20 per ₹100 of face value. The dirty price is ₹99.70, so buying ₹10 lakh of face value costs ₹9,97,000.
formula: Clean price = Dirty price − Accrued interest

short: The full amount a bond buyer actually pays: the quoted clean price plus the interest earned since the last coupon payment.
kid: It's the total you pay at the toy shop once the toy and its batteries are both added up.
detail: The dirty price, also called the full or invoice price, is the present value of all a bond's remaining cash flows, and it is the amount that changes hands at settlement. It equals the clean price plus accrued interest. Between coupon dates the dirty price rises steadily as interest builds up, then falls by roughly the coupon amount on the payment date, creating a saw-tooth pattern even when yields do not move. That is why markets quote the clean price and add accrued interest only at settlement. For valuation, discounting a bond's future cash flows at its yield gives the dirty price, not the clean one. Common confusion: a drop in the dirty price just after a coupon date is not a loss; the holder has received that value as cash.
example: Say ₹50 lakh of face value of a bond is quoted at a clean price of ₹101.00 with accrued interest of ₹2.10 per ₹100. The dirty price is ₹103.10, so the buyer pays ₹51,55,000.
formula: Dirty price = Clean price + Accrued interest

short: A bond with no maturity date: the issuer pays interest indefinitely and never has to repay the principal, though it may choose to.
kid: Imagine a friend borrows your toy car and, instead of ever giving it back, gives you one sweet every week forever.
detail: A perpetual bond pays a fixed or floating coupon with no final maturity. Investors earn only the coupon stream unless the issuer calls the bond, which most modern perpetuals allow after five or ten years. Because the principal never has to be repaid, rating agencies and regulators often treat perpetuals as partly equity-like; banks issue them as Additional Tier 1 capital, and some companies use them to strengthen their balance sheets. The UK government's consols, first issued in the 18th century, were the classic example until the Treasury redeemed the last of them in 2015. Perpetuals are highly sensitive to interest rates, and investors carry call risk and, in bank versions, write-down risk. Common confusion: 'perpetual' does not mean the investor is locked in forever; the bonds can be sold in the market, at whatever price it offers.
example: Say a perpetual bond pays a $50 coupon every year. If investors want a 5% yield, it is worth $50 / 0.05 = $1,000; if the required yield rises to 6%, its value falls to $50 / 0.06 = $833.33, a drop of about 16.7%.
formula: Price = Annual coupon / Required yield

short: A perpetual bank bond that counts as capital and can be written down or turned into shares if the bank gets into trouble.
kid: Imagine you give crayons to keep a friend's art club going. If the club starts falling apart, your crayons get used up to save it, and you may not get them back.
detail: Additional Tier 1 (AT1) bonds are a Basel III instrument that lets banks raise loss-absorbing capital without issuing ordinary shares. They are perpetual, usually callable after five years with regulatory approval, and the bank can skip coupons without it counting as a default. If the bank's common equity ratio falls below a trigger, or the regulator judges the bank non-viable, the bonds are written down or converted into equity. Because of these triggers they are often called contingent convertibles (CoCos), though not every CoCo is an AT1. Investors earn a higher coupon for this risk. In March 2020, Yes Bank's AT1 bonds of about ₹8,400 crore were written off, a decision later fought in court, and in March 2023 about CHF 16 billion of Credit Suisse AT1s were wiped out while shareholders kept some value. Common confusion: AT1s are not safe deposits or ordinary senior bonds.
example: Say ABC Bank issues ₹1,000 crore of AT1 bonds at an 8.5% coupon, costing it ₹85 crore a year. If its common equity ratio falls below the trigger and the bonds are written down by half, investors' claim shrinks to ₹500 crore and future coupons fall to ₹42.5 crore a year.

short: A bond whose money must be spent on projects that help the environment, such as solar power, clean transport or energy efficiency.
kid: It's like collecting coins from friends and promising to spend every single one on planting trees in the park.
detail: A green bond is an ordinary bond, with the same credit risk as the issuer's other debt, whose proceeds are earmarked for eligible environmental projects. Issuers usually follow the ICMA Green Bond Principles: they define eligible projects, track the money, report on its use and often obtain an external review. The European Investment Bank issued the first such bond, its Climate Awareness Bond, in 2007, and the market has since grown to include sovereigns, banks and companies. India issued its first sovereign green bonds in January and February 2023, raising ₹16,000 crore in two tranches. Investors with environmental mandates sometimes accept a slightly lower yield, called the greenium. Common confusion: 'green' describes the use of the money, not the issuer, so a fossil-fuel company can issue a green bond, which is why independent verification and greenwashing scrutiny matter.
example: Say ABC Power issues ₹500 crore of 10-year green bonds at 7.30% while its regular 10-year bonds yield 7.40%. The 10-basis-point greenium saves it ₹50 lakh a year in interest (₹500 crore × 0.10%).

short: A bond sold to overseas investors but denominated in Indian rupees, so the foreign investor, not the Indian issuer, bears the currency risk.
kid: Imagine you borrow toys from a friend far away and promise to give back sweets from your own town. If those sweets become less special there, your friend feels it, not you.
detail: A masala bond is issued outside India, typically listed in London, Singapore or on an exchange in GIFT City's IFSC, but its principal and coupons are in rupees, usually settled in dollars at the prevailing exchange rate. The International Finance Corporation coined the name, an Indian cooking word, in 2014 for offshore rupee bonds it listed in London. Indian companies, banks and bodies such as NHAI have used them under RBI's external commercial borrowing rules. For the issuer, the advantage is avoiding currency risk: if the rupee weakens, its repayment in rupees is unchanged, whereas a dollar bond would cost more. Foreign investors take that risk in exchange for higher rupee yields, and issuance has stayed modest because they demand a premium for it. Common confusion: a masala bond is not issued in India; it is an offshore bond in rupees.
example: Say ABC Ltd issues ₹1,000 crore of masala bonds when $1 = ₹80, so investors pay $125 million. If the rupee weakens to ₹100 per dollar by maturity, ABC still repays ₹1,000 crore, but investors receive only $100 million, a 20% currency loss before coupons.

aliases: Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal of Securities
hl: separate trading of registered interest and principal
short: Zero-coupon securities created by separating a bond's individual interest payments and its principal repayment, so each can be traded on its own.
kid: Imagine a chocolate bar with many small squares and one big square at the end. You snap it apart so different friends can each take the piece they want.
detail: STRIPS (Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal of Securities) are created by splitting a coupon-paying government bond into its separate cash flows. Each coupon becomes a coupon strip and the face value becomes a principal strip; each pays a single amount on one date, so it trades at a discount like a zero-coupon bond. The US Treasury has run its STRIPS programme since 1985, and the RBI permits stripping and reconstitution of eligible government securities. Strips appeal to pension funds and insurers that need cash on exact future dates. Because they pay no coupons, their Macaulay duration equals their maturity, making long strips very sensitive to rates. Common confusion: STRIPS are not sold directly by the government; dealers create them from existing bonds and can recombine them into the original bond, a process called reconstitution.
example: Say a ₹100 face value G-sec with two years left pays a 7% coupon half-yearly. Stripping it creates four coupon strips of ₹3.50 each and one principal strip of ₹100; together the five pieces promise ₹114, exactly the original bond's remaining cash flows.
formula: Price of a strip = Cash flow / (1 + y/2)^(2t), where y is the annual yield and t the years to payment

short: A Government of India bond priced in grams of gold that pays fixed interest and is repaid at the market price of gold.
kid: Imagine a promise card from the grown-ups that says it will be worth one shiny gold coin later, and they also give you a little treat every year for keeping it.
detail: Sovereign gold bonds (SGBs) are issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India, denominated in grams of gold and redeemed in rupees at the prevailing gold price. Launched in November 2015 to reduce physical gold imports, they have an eight-year tenure with an early exit option from the fifth year, can be traded on stock exchanges, and pay a fixed 2.5% a year on the initial investment. Under the rules as of 2025, the interest is taxable, but capital gains on redemption at maturity are exempt for individuals. As of 2025, no new tranches had been issued since February 2024, so investors buy existing SGBs on exchanges. Common confusion: SGBs remove storage and purity worries, but not price risk; if gold falls, the redemption value falls, and when gold surges, the government's own repayment cost rises sharply.
example: Say you bought 10 grams of SGBs at ₹5,000 per gram, ₹50,000 in all. You would receive 2.5% of ₹50,000, or ₹1,250, each year in two half-yearly payments; if gold is ₹9,000 per gram at maturity, you get back ₹90,000.
formula: Redemption value = Grams held × Gold price at redemption (RBI reference price)

short: A bond issued by a city, town or other local government body to pay for public works such as water supply, roads or sewers.
kid: Imagine your town wants a new playground, so it borrows coins from families and promises to give them back, with a little extra, over the years.
detail: Municipal bonds are debt issued by local governments and their agencies. In the US, a market worth trillions of dollars, interest on most munis is exempt from federal income tax, so investors compare them using a tax-equivalent yield. They are either general obligation bonds, backed by the issuer's taxing power, or revenue bonds, repaid from a specific project such as a toll road. India's market is small: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation issued the first municipal bond without a state guarantee in 1998, SEBI framed issue rules in 2015, and Pune, Indore, Hyderabad and other cities have since raised money, helped by central government incentives. Their ability to borrow depends on sound municipal finances and credit ratings. Common confusion: municipal bonds are not backed by the national government; a city can and occasionally does default, as Detroit did in its 2013 bankruptcy.
example: Say a US muni yields 3.5% tax-free and you are in a 35% tax bracket. Its tax-equivalent yield is 3.5% / (1 − 0.35) ≈ 5.38%, so a taxable bond must yield more than that to beat it.
formula: Tax-equivalent yield = Tax-free yield / (1 − Marginal tax rate)

short: A bond whose interest income is exempt from income tax for the investor, so a lower coupon can still beat a taxable bond.
kid: Usually, when you earn a sweet, your big brother takes a bite. With this special jar, he isn't allowed to take any.
detail: A tax-free bond pays interest that is exempt from income tax. In India, such bonds were issued mainly between 2011-12 and 2015-16 by government-backed entities such as NHAI, REC, PFC, IRFC and HUDCO, with tenures of 10, 15 or 20 years. Their interest is exempt from income tax under Section 10 of the Income-tax Act, under the rules as of 2025, although any capital gain on selling them is taxed. No fresh issues have come since 2016, so investors buy them on the NSE and BSE, often at a premium to face value. Their appeal rises with the investor's tax slab, since the exemption is worth more to someone paying 30% than to someone paying nothing. Common confusion: 'tax-free' covers the interest only; it does not make the price fixed or the investment risk-free, and the real yield depends on the price paid.
example: Say you hold ₹10 lakh of a 7% tax-free bond and pay tax at 30% (ignoring cess). You keep the full ₹70,000 interest each year, whereas a 9% taxable bond would pay ₹90,000 but leave you ₹63,000 after tax; to match the tax-free bond, a taxable bond would need to yield 7% / (1 − 0.30) = 10%.
formula: Pre-tax equivalent yield = Tax-free yield / (1 − Tax rate)

short: A bond in which Indians can invest the profit from selling land or a building, so that profit escapes long-term capital gains tax.
kid: Imagine you sell your old bicycle and get extra coins. If you put those coins in a special locked box for a few years, nobody takes a share of them.
detail: Capital gains bonds, commonly called 54EC bonds, let an investor claim exemption from tax on long-term capital gains from the sale of land or buildings, by investing the gain in notified bonds within six months of the sale. Under the rules as of 2025, the issuers are government-backed entities such as REC, PFC and IRFC, investment is capped at ₹50 lakh across the financial year of the sale and the next one, the lock-in is five years, and the bonds cannot be transferred. The interest is modest and taxable, so the real benefit is the tax saved on the gain. They suit people who sell property and do not plan to buy another home, since Sections 54 and 54F offer alternatives for reinvesting in a house. Common confusion: 54EC bonds cover gains from land or buildings only, not gains from shares or mutual funds.
example: Say you sell a plot and make a long-term capital gain of ₹60 lakh. If you invest the maximum ₹50 lakh in 54EC bonds within six months, that ₹50 lakh of gain is exempt and only the remaining ₹10 lakh is taxed, under the rules as of 2025.

short: A bond issued in a currency other than that of the country where it is sold, such as a US dollar bond sold in London.
kid: Imagine you take your toys to a fair in another town, and everyone there agrees to swap using stickers from a third town altogether.
detail: A Eurobond is an international bond underwritten by a global group of banks and sold to investors outside the home market of its currency, for example a US dollar bond sold in London and Singapore, or a yen bond sold in Europe. The market began in 1963 with a dollar bond for Italy's Autostrade, arranged in London, and grew because issuers could avoid some national registration rules and withholding taxes. Today it is the main channel for large companies, banks and governments to borrow internationally; Indian companies and state-owned firms sell dollar bonds this way under RBI's external borrowing rules. Common confusion: 'Euro' means offshore, not the euro currency or Europe, so a dollar bond sold in Tokyo is still a Eurobond. It also differs from a foreign bond, issued inside the currency's home market, and from the jointly issued EU debt sometimes called eurobonds.
example: Say ABC Ltd, an Indian company, sells $500 million of five-year dollar bonds to investors in London and Singapore at a 5% coupon. It pays $25 million in interest a year; if the rupee weakens from ₹80 to ₹88 per dollar, that interest costs ₹220 crore instead of ₹200 crore.

short: A bond issued by a foreign borrower in another country's home market and currency, such as a Japanese company selling dollar bonds in the US.
kid: Imagine a child from another school sets up a stall at your school's fair, following your school's rules and using your school's tokens.
detail: A foreign bond is sold in a country's domestic market, in that country's currency, by an issuer from abroad, and it must follow local securities rules. Many have nicknames: Yankee bonds are dollar bonds sold in the US by non-US issuers, Samurai bonds are yen bonds in Japan, Bulldog bonds are sterling bonds in the UK, and Panda bonds are renminbi bonds in China. Issuers use them to tap a deep investor base, to raise money in a currency they need for local operations, or to match revenues in that currency. They differ from Eurobonds, which are sold outside the home market of their currency. In India, the parallel is a foreign entity issuing rupee bonds onshore, as some multilateral lenders have done. Common confusion: 'foreign' describes the issuer, not the currency; the bond is in the local currency of the market where it is sold.
example: Say ABC Corp, a hypothetical Indian company, sells ¥10 billion of five-year Samurai bonds in Tokyo at a 1.2% coupon. It pays ¥120 million in interest each year to Japanese investors and must follow Japan's disclosure rules.

short: When a global bond index adds a country's government bonds, prompting funds that track that index to buy them.
kid: Imagine the popular list of favourite games adds your game. Suddenly lots of children who follow the list come to play it.
detail: Global bond indices, such as JP Morgan's GBI-EM, the Bloomberg Emerging Markets Local Currency Government Index and FTSE Russell's emerging markets government bond index, admit countries based on size, liquidity, market access and settlement. When a country is added, funds that track or benchmark against the index must buy its bonds, usually in phases over several months. India's government bonds issued under the Fully Accessible Route joined the JP Morgan GBI-EM from June 2024, with the weight rising by one percentage point a month to 10% by March 2025, Bloomberg began a phased inclusion in January 2025, and FTSE Russell followed from September 2025. Inclusion brings steady foreign demand, which can lower yields and support the rupee, but it also ties the market more closely to global fund flows, which can reverse quickly. Common confusion: inclusion does not guarantee permanently lower borrowing costs.
example: Say $240 billion of funds track an index and India's weight is set at 10%. Those funds would need to buy about $24 billion of Indian government bonds; spread over 10 monthly steps, that is roughly $2.4 billion of buying a month.
formula: Passive inflow ≈ Assets tracking the index × Country's index weight

short: An RBI channel that lets non-residents buy specified Indian government bonds without any limit on the amount.
kid: Imagine a special gate at the playground that lets visiting children walk in and play on certain swings as much as they like, with no waiting list.
detail: The Fully Accessible Route (FAR) was announced by the RBI in March 2020 and opened in April 2020 as a separate channel for non-resident investors, alongside the general route for foreign portfolio investors and the Voluntary Retention Route. Under FAR, specified central government securities, including the 5-, 10- and 30-year benchmark bonds and other tenors added later, are open to non-residents with no quantitative cap, and a bond once designated stays eligible until maturity. FAR was central to India's inclusion in global bond indices, because index providers require unrestricted foreign access. Foreign holdings of FAR bonds are published regularly and watched as a gauge of overseas demand. Common confusion: FAR does not open all Indian bonds to unlimited foreign buying; under the rules as of 2025, state government bonds, corporate bonds and non-designated G-secs remain under the Medium Term Framework limits.
example: Say an overseas pension fund wants ₹5,000 crore of Indian government bonds. Through FAR it can buy the whole amount in designated 10-year G-secs without using up any FPI limit; at a 7% coupon, that earns ₹350 crore of interest a year.

short: The process by which a government or central bank sells new bonds to investors, with prices or yields set by competing bids.
kid: Imagine the class sells its last cupcakes by asking everyone how many coins they would give, and the best offers get the cupcakes.
detail: Governments raise most of their borrowing through regular auctions. In India the RBI conducts auctions of central government securities, state development loans and Treasury bills on its E-Kuber platform, following an indicative half-yearly calendar. Banks, primary dealers, insurers and others submit competitive bids stating a price or yield and an amount; small investors can place non-competitive bids, filled at the weighted average price. Bids are accepted from the best level downwards until the notified amount is filled, and the last accepted level is the cut-off. Auctions can be uniform-price, where all winners pay the cut-off price, or multiple-price, where each pays its own bid; the RBI uses both. Results such as the cut-off yield, bid-to-cover ratio and any devolvement are read closely as signals of demand. Common confusion: an auction sells new bonds; existing bonds trade in the secondary market.
example: Say the RBI offers ₹10,000 crore of a 10-year bond and receives bids of ₹4,000 crore at 6.90%, ₹5,000 crore at 6.92% and ₹3,000 crore at 6.95%. It accepts the first two in full (₹9,000 crore) and ₹1,000 crore of the 6.95% bids, so the cut-off yield is 6.95% and one-third of those bids are filled.

short: The highest yield, or lowest price, an issuer accepts in a bond auction; every accepted bid is at or better than this level.
kid: When the class sells cupcakes to the best offers, the smallest offer that still gets a cupcake marks the line. Anyone offering less goes home without one.
detail: In a bond auction, bids are ranked from the lowest yield (highest price) upwards and accepted until the notified amount is filled; the yield of the last accepted bid is the cut-off yield, and the matching price is the cut-off price. Bids at exactly that level may be filled only in part. For a newly issued Indian G-sec, the cut-off yield usually becomes the bond's coupon. Traders compare the cut-off with secondary-market yields just before the auction: a cut-off above market levels signals weak demand, while one below signals strong demand. The issuer can also reject bids it considers too expensive, keeping the cut-off lower and selling less, which may trigger devolvement. Common confusion: in Indian share IPOs, 'cut-off price' means the final issue price fixed through book building, a different concept.
example: Say the RBI offers ₹12,000 crore and gets bids of ₹6,000 crore at 7.00%, ₹5,000 crore at 7.02% and ₹4,000 crore at 7.04%. It needs ₹1,000 crore from the 7.04% bids, so the cut-off yield is 7.04% and those bidders receive 25% of what they asked for.

short: The total amount bid in an auction divided by the amount actually sold; a higher number means stronger demand.
kid: If the class has 10 cupcakes and 25 children put up their hands for one, far more children want cupcakes than there are cupcakes.
detail: The bid-to-cover ratio measures demand in a securities auction by comparing the value of all bids received with the value accepted. A ratio of 2.5 means bids were two and a half times the amount sold. It is published for US Treasury auctions and for RBI auctions of G-secs, state development loans and Treasury bills, and traders compare it with recent auctions of the same maturity rather than with a fixed threshold. A falling ratio can signal waning appetite for a government's debt, while a high one shows depth. It is best read together with the cut-off yield or auction tail and the mix of bidders. Common confusion: a high bid-to-cover does not guarantee a good price for the issuer, since many bids may have been at unattractive yields far from the cut-off.
example: Say the US Treasury sells $42 billion of 10-year notes and receives $105 billion of bids. The bid-to-cover ratio is $105 billion / $42 billion = 2.5.
formula: Bid-to-cover ratio = Total amount bid / Amount accepted

short: A bank or firm appointed by the central bank to bid in government bond auctions, underwrite them and keep the bonds actively traded.
kid: Imagine a few trusted helpers at the school fair who promise to buy any cupcakes nobody else wants, and who keep swapping treats so the fair stays busy.
detail: Primary dealers are authorised intermediaries in the government securities market. In India the RBI appoints both standalone primary dealers and banks that run a primary dealership business. They must underwrite government bond auctions through a minimum underwriting commitment plus additional competitive underwriting bids, bid in Treasury bill auctions, quote two-way prices in the secondary market, and help distribute bonds to investors. In return they get access to RBI liquidity support and earn underwriting commission. In the US, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York designates primary dealers that must bid in every Treasury auction and act as counterparties in monetary policy operations. They matter because they ensure auctions are covered, which keeps government borrowing reliable. Common confusion: primary dealers are not the government's only buyers; banks, insurers and mutual funds also bid, and dealers act mainly as a backstop and market-maker.
example: Say 20 primary dealers share a minimum underwriting commitment covering half of a ₹12,000 crore auction. Each must underwrite ₹6,000 crore / 20 = ₹300 crore, and any part left unsold devolves on them in proportion to their commitments.

short: When a government bond auction is not fully bought by investors, the unsold part is passed to the underwriting primary dealers to buy.
kid: If the class can't sell all its cupcakes, the helpers who promised to take the leftovers must carry them home.
detail: Devolvement happens when a government securities auction attracts too few acceptable bids, or when the RBI rejects bids it considers too high in yield, leaving part of the notified amount unsold. Primary dealers that underwrote the auction must then take up the shortfall at the cut-off price, in proportion to their underwriting commitments. It signals that the market wanted a higher yield than the RBI was willing to pay, and dealers end up holding bonds that may fall in price. Devolvement is reported in auction results and is read as a sign of weak demand and of the RBI's yield preference. Before April 2006 the RBI itself could buy unsold government debt in auctions; the FRBM Act ended that. Common confusion: devolvement is not the same as cancelling an auction; the RBI can separately cancel or reduce an issue, which leaves nothing to devolve.
example: Say the RBI notifies ₹10,000 crore of a 10-year G-sec but accepts only ₹7,600 crore of bids at yields it finds reasonable. The remaining ₹2,400 crore devolves on primary dealers; a dealer with 10% of the underwriting commitment must buy ₹240 crore.
formula: Devolvement = Notified amount − Amount accepted from bids

short: The RBI's electronic platform where banks, primary dealers and other members trade Indian government bonds anonymously by matching orders.
kid: Imagine a big board where children pin up what they want to swap, and a fair helper matches them up without showing anyone's name.
detail: The Negotiated Dealing System-Order Matching (NDS-OM) is an anonymous, screen-based system for secondary-market trading in government securities, owned by the RBI and launched in 2005. Banks, primary dealers, insurers, mutual funds and other regulated entities place buy and sell orders, quoted as clean prices, and the system matches them by price and then time. Trades are settled through the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL), which acts as central counterparty, normally on T+1. Most outright trading in G-secs happens on NDS-OM, and its prices feed published benchmark yields. Retail investors reach it through brokers and banks and, since 2021, directly through RBI Retail Direct. Common confusion: NDS-OM is for trading existing bonds; new government bonds are sold through RBI auctions on the separate E-Kuber platform.
example: Say a bank buys ₹50 crore face value of the 10-year benchmark on NDS-OM at a clean price of ₹101.25. It pays ₹50.625 crore plus accrued interest, and the trade settles through CCIL on the next working day.

short: An RBI scheme that lets individuals open a free account with the central bank and buy government bonds directly, without a broker.
kid: Imagine you could walk straight to the head teacher's office to get special stickers, instead of asking an older child to fetch them for you.
detail: RBI Retail Direct, launched in November 2021, lets resident individuals and eligible non-residents open a Retail Direct Gilt (RDG) account with the RBI online at no charge. Through it they can bid non-competitively in primary auctions of central government securities, Treasury bills and state development loans, receiving the weighted average auction price, and buy or sell existing bonds on the NDS-OM platform. Coupons and maturity proceeds go straight to the linked bank account. The scheme put India among the few countries where individuals can buy government bonds directly from the central bank, and gives savers a sovereign, default-free alternative to bank deposits. Common confusion: government bonds carry no credit risk but do carry interest-rate risk; selling a long bond early after yields rise can mean a loss, and buyers for small lots can be scarce.
example: Say you invest ₹1 lakh through a non-competitive bid in a 10-year G-sec with a 7% coupon and receive it at face value. You get ₹3,500 every six months, ₹70,000 over ten years, and your ₹1 lakh back at maturity.

short: The most recently issued government bond of a given maturity, usually the most actively traded and the market's benchmark for that maturity.
kid: It's like the newest toy in the shop window that every child talks about, while last year's version still works but sits further back on the shelf.
detail: When a government issues a new bond of a standard maturity, such as 10 years, that issue becomes on-the-run, and earlier issues of similar maturity become off-the-run. On-the-run securities attract the most trading, have the tightest bid-ask spreads and serve as benchmarks for pricing other bonds and derivatives. Because investors pay for that liquidity, on-the-run bonds usually yield slightly less than comparable off-the-run bonds, a gap traders call the on-the-run premium. In India, the newest 10-year G-sec becomes the benchmark once it has been reissued to a meaningful size, and the benchmark yield quoted in the news refers to it. Relative-value funds trade the gap, betting it will narrow as the new bond ages. Common confusion: off-the-run bonds are not riskier in credit terms; they are the same government's debt, only less liquid.
example: Say the new 10-year G-sec yields 6.33% while an older bond maturing within months of it yields 6.38%. The 5-basis-point gap is the on-the-run premium; a trader who buys the older bond and sells the newer one profits if that gap narrows.

short: The market where governments, companies and other borrowers sell debt securities, and investors buy and trade them.
kid: Imagine a place where children who need to borrow toys meet friends happy to lend them, in return for a little thank-you treat each week.
detail: The bond market, also called the debt or fixed-income market, covers the primary market, where new bonds are sold through auctions or placements, and the secondary market, where existing bonds trade, mostly over the counter between institutions. Globally it is roughly as large as, or larger than, the stock market, and government bond yields set the base cost of money for home loans, company borrowing and valuations. In India the market is dominated by government securities, held largely by banks, insurers, provident funds and the RBI, with trading on NDS-OM; corporate bonds trade on NSE and BSE platforms and are mostly privately placed. Bond prices move opposite to yields, so rising interest rates cause losses for existing holders. Common confusion: bonds are not risk-free; they carry interest-rate, credit, inflation and liquidity risks that vary by issuer and maturity.
example: Say a bond will pay ₹107 in one year (₹100 face value plus a ₹7 coupon) and the market yield is 7%, so it trades at ₹100. If market yields rise to 8%, its price falls to ₹107 / 1.08 = ₹99.07.
formula: Bond price = Sum of [Cash flow at time t / (1 + y)^t]

short: An arrangement in which a bond issuer sets aside money or retires part of its bonds at intervals before maturity, reducing repayment risk.
kid: Imagine saving a few coins in a jar every week, so that when your big birthday party comes, you already have enough to pay for it.
detail: A sinking fund provision in a bond indenture requires the issuer to repay part of the principal before maturity, either by depositing money with a trustee or by retiring a set amount of bonds each year. The issuer can usually choose between buying bonds in the market, which is cheaper when they trade below face value, or calling them at par, often chosen by lottery. Because the debt shrinks gradually, credit risk is lower and investors may accept a slightly lower yield. In India, state governments maintain a Consolidated Sinking Fund with the RBI to meet future repayments of their market loans. Common confusion: a sinking fund is not always good for investors; if rates fall and the bonds trade above par, the issuer can redeem some at par, and those holders lose a high-coupon bond. In accounting, the term can also mean any reserve for a future expense.
example: Say ABC Ltd issues ₹500 crore of 10-year bonds with a sinking fund that retires ₹50 crore a year in years 6 to 9. That repays ₹200 crore early, leaving ₹300 crore to be repaid at maturity in year 10.
formula: Annual deposit = Target amount × r / ((1 + r)^n − 1), where r is the rate earned on deposits and n the number of years

short: A bond that repays its principal in instalments over its life, along with interest, instead of all at once at maturity.
kid: Imagine borrowing a whole pack of stickers and giving a few back every week, plus one extra as a thank-you, until the pack is all returned.
detail: An amortising bond returns principal gradually according to a schedule, so each payment contains interest on the outstanding balance plus part of the principal, and interest payments shrink as the balance falls. This contrasts with a bullet bond, which pays only coupons until the full face value is repaid at maturity. Amortising structures suit borrowers whose cash comes in steadily, such as infrastructure projects, and are common in mortgage-backed and other asset-backed securities. For investors, they reduce credit exposure over time and have a shorter weighted average life and duration than a bullet bond with the same final maturity, but they create reinvestment risk because money comes back early. Common confusion: the final maturity overstates how long your money is tied up; use the weighted average life instead. It is also different from the accounting idea of amortising a bond premium.
example: Say a ₹30 lakh, three-year bond pays 10% a year and repays ₹10 lakh of principal each year. Year 1 pays ₹10 lakh + ₹3 lakh interest = ₹13 lakh, year 2 pays ₹10 lakh + ₹2 lakh = ₹12 lakh, and year 3 pays ₹10 lakh + ₹1 lakh = ₹11 lakh.
formula: Interest for a period = Coupon rate × Outstanding principal at the start of the period

short: A bond whose coupon rises to higher, pre-set levels on scheduled dates, or after a specified event such as a rating downgrade.
kid: Imagine a friend who gives you one sweet a week this month, two a week next month and three after that, just as you agreed at the start.
detail: A step-up bond pays a coupon that increases according to a schedule written into its terms, for example 6% for two years, then 7%, then 8%. Many are callable, and the issuer tends to redeem them at a call date if rates have fallen or its credit has improved, so investors may never receive the higher coupons. Other versions step up only on an event, such as a credit-rating downgrade or a missed target in a sustainability-linked bond. Step-ups keep the issuer's early interest costs low and give investors some protection if rates rise. Common confusion: a step-up bond is not a floating rate bond; its future coupons are fixed in advance and do not track market rates. Under Basel III, bank capital instruments may not include step-ups, because they create an incentive to redeem early.
example: Say a ₹10 lakh five-year step-up bond pays 6% in years 1 and 2, 7% in years 3 and 4 and 8% in year 5. Total interest is ₹60,000 + ₹60,000 + ₹70,000 + ₹70,000 + ₹80,000 = ₹3,40,000, an average of 6.8% a year.

short: The legal contract between a bond issuer and its bondholders that sets out the bond's terms, the issuer's promises and investors' rights.
kid: It's like the rules you and a friend write down before you lend your favourite toy: when it comes back, and what happens if it breaks.
detail: A bond indenture, called a trust deed in India and the UK, is the formal agreement governing a bond issue. It specifies the principal, coupon, payment dates, maturity, call and put features, any security or collateral, ranking against other debt, events of default and the remedies available. It also contains covenants: affirmative ones, such as maintaining insurance and filing accounts, and negative ones, such as limits on extra borrowing, asset sales or dividends. A trustee, usually a bank or trust company, monitors compliance and acts for bondholders, who are too many to negotiate individually. In India, a SEBI-registered debenture trustee executes the debenture trust deed. Covenants matter because they stop a company from taking on more risk after borrowing. Common confusion: the prospectus or offer document markets the bond, but the indenture is the binding contract that courts enforce.
example: Say ABC Ltd's indenture for ₹300 crore of bonds requires net debt to stay below 3.5 times EBITDA. If EBITDA is ₹100 crore and net debt rises to ₹380 crore, the ratio is 3.8 times, a covenant breach that lets the trustee seek remedies.

short: A set of bonds bought to mature at evenly spaced dates, so money comes back regularly and can be reinvested.
kid: Imagine planting seeds that bloom at different times, so you get a fresh flower to pick every year instead of all at once.
detail: A bond ladder spreads an investment across bonds or deposits with staggered maturities, such as one, two, three, four and five years. When the shortest bond matures, the money is reinvested at the long end of the ladder, keeping the structure intact. Laddering reduces the risk of reinvesting everything at a single, possibly low, interest rate, gives predictable cash flow, and lowers price sensitivity compared with putting everything into the longest bond. Individuals build ladders with G-secs, corporate bonds, fixed deposits or target maturity funds, and retirement planners use them to match spending needs. Common confusion: a ladder does not remove interest-rate risk; it averages it over time. Bonds sold before maturity can still lose value, and a ladder of weak issuers still carries their credit risk.
example: Say you split ₹10 lakh equally into bonds maturing in 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 years, ₹2 lakh each. Every year ₹2 lakh matures and is reinvested in a new five-year bond, so one rung of the ladder always comes due each year.

short: A bond portfolio that holds mostly very short-term and very long-term bonds, with little or nothing in between.
kid: Imagine keeping some sweets to eat today and some saved for a long, long time from now, and none for the days in between.
detail: In a barbell strategy, an investor concentrates holdings at the two ends of the maturity range, for example one-year bills and twenty-year bonds. The short end offers liquidity and the chance to reinvest if rates rise, while the long end locks in yields and gains in price if rates fall. The contrasting bullet strategy concentrates holdings around a single maturity, and a ladder spreads them evenly. For the same duration, a barbell has more convexity than a bullet, so it tends to do better when yields move sharply or the yield curve flattens, and worse when the curve steepens. The term is also used beyond bonds, for pairing very safe assets with a small slice of very risky ones. Common confusion: a barbell's average maturity can match a ten-year bond, yet it behaves differently because its two ends react differently to shifts in the curve.
example: Say you put ₹5 lakh in a 1-year bill and ₹5 lakh in a 19-year bond. The simple average maturity is (0.5 × 1) + (0.5 × 19) = 10 years, the same as putting ₹10 lakh into one 10-year bond, but the barbell responds differently when short and long yields move.

short: Arranging a bond portfolio so its value will cover a known future payment however interest rates move.
kid: Imagine a seesaw built so that when one side goes up, the other goes down by the same amount, and the snack bowl in the middle never spills.
detail: Immunisation protects a portfolio against interest-rate changes by balancing two opposing effects. When rates rise, bond prices fall but coupons can be reinvested at higher rates; when rates fall, the reverse happens. By setting the portfolio's Macaulay duration equal to the investment horizon, and its present value equal to that of the liability, the two effects roughly cancel for small, parallel rate shifts. The assets' convexity should also be at least that of the liabilities, so small rate moves leave a surplus rather than a shortfall. Pension funds and insurers use it to make sure promised payouts can be met. The idea was formalised by the actuary Frank Redington in 1952. Common confusion: immunisation is not a one-time setup. Duration drifts as time passes and rates change, so the portfolio needs regular rebalancing, and it does not protect against defaults or large, uneven moves in the yield curve.
example: Say a pension fund owes ₹100 crore in exactly 7 years and yields are 7%. It needs ₹100 crore / (1.07)^7 ≈ ₹62.27 crore today, invested in bonds with a portfolio Macaulay duration of 7 years, such as a 7-year zero-coupon G-sec strip.
formula: PV(assets) = PV(liabilities); Duration(assets) = Duration(liabilities); Convexity(assets) ≥ Convexity(liabilities)

short: Bond investors who sell a government's bonds, pushing up its borrowing costs, to protest against policies they see as reckless.
kid: Imagine children who stop sharing their toys with a friend who keeps breaking them, until that friend promises to be more careful.
detail: The term bond vigilantes was coined by economist Ed Yardeni in the 1980s for investors who discipline governments and central banks by selling bonds when they fear excessive deficits, inflation or unsound policy. The selling drives yields up, raising the government's cost of borrowing and pressuring it to change course. Well-known episodes include the 1994 global bond sell-off and the reaction to the UK's September 2022 mini-budget, after which long-dated gilt yields jumped, the Bank of England stepped in to buy gilts, and Prime Minister Liz Truss resigned within weeks. In emerging markets such as India, the reaction often shows up through foreign outflows and the currency as well as yields. Common confusion: the vigilantes are not an organised group; the term describes the market's collective reaction, and yields can also rise for reasons unrelated to fiscal worries.
example: Say a government announces large unfunded spending and investors sell its 10-year bonds, lifting the yield from 4.0% to 4.5%. On $100 billion of new borrowing, that adds $500 million a year in interest cost ($100 billion × 0.5%).

short: A bond's extra yield over the risk-free curve after removing the value of any built-in option, such as the issuer's right to repay early.
kid: A friend gives you extra sweets for borrowing your bike, but some of those sweets are really for being allowed to return it whenever they like. Take those away, and what's left is your true reward.
detail: The option-adjusted spread (OAS) is the constant spread that, added to the benchmark government or swap curve across many simulated interest-rate paths, makes a model's price equal the bond's market price. It is used for bonds with embedded options, such as callable corporate bonds and mortgage-backed securities, whose cash flows change as rates move. A related measure, the Z-spread, is the constant spread over the zero-coupon (spot) curve that discounts the bond's promised cash flows to its price, ignoring options. For a callable bond the investor has effectively sold an option to the issuer, so the OAS is lower than the Z-spread; for a putable bond it is higher. OAS lets analysts compare credit and liquidity compensation across bonds with different features. Common confusion: OAS depends on the model's volatility assumption, so different systems can give different values for the same bond.
example: Say a callable corporate bond has a Z-spread of 180 basis points and a model values the issuer's call option at 45 basis points. Its OAS is 180 − 45 = 135 basis points, the spread actually earned for credit and liquidity risk.
formula: OAS = Z-spread − Option cost (for a callable bond)

short: The difference between a bond's yield and the yield of a government bond with the same maturity, showing the extra reward for its risk.
kid: If the most trusted child in class borrows crayons for one sweet, but a forgetful child must offer three sweets, the two extra sweets are for the worry.
detail: The G-spread measures how much more a bond yields than a government bond of the same maturity, usually interpolated from the government yield curve when no exact match exists. Because government bonds in their own currency are treated as free of default risk, the G-spread reflects compensation for credit risk, liquidity and features such as call options. In India, corporate bonds are commonly quoted as a spread over the G-sec of similar tenor; globally, spreads over Treasuries are standard. The I-spread is the same idea measured against the interest-rate swap curve, which banks often use for hedging. Spreads widen in stress and narrow in calm markets, so credit investors track them closely. Common confusion: the G-spread is not purely default risk; it also captures liquidity and tax differences, and it ignores the shape of the curve, which the Z-spread and option-adjusted spread handle better.
example: Say an AAA-rated 5-year corporate bond yields 7.45% and the 5-year G-sec yields 6.60%. The G-spread is 7.45% − 6.60% = 0.85%, or 85 basis points.
formula: G-spread = Bond yield − Interpolated government bond yield of the same maturity

short: A bank bond backed by a ring-fenced pool of high-quality loans, giving investors a claim on both the bank and the pool.
kid: Imagine a friend borrows your toys and puts their best teddy in a locked box. If they can't give your toys back, you get to keep the teddy.
detail: A covered bond is a senior debt instrument, typically issued by a bank and backed by a dedicated cover pool of assets such as home loans or public-sector loans. Unlike securitisation, the assets stay on the bank's balance sheet and investors have dual recourse: first to the issuing bank and, if it fails, to the cover pool, which is legally ring-fenced. Issuers must keep the pool larger than the bonds, called overcollateralisation, and replace weak assets. Germany's Pfandbriefe trace back to 18th-century Prussia, and covered bonds remain a major funding source for European banks, often carrying AAA ratings and low yields. They are rare in India, where banks rely more on deposits. Common confusion: covered bonds are not mortgage-backed securities; in an MBS the loans are sold to a separate vehicle and investors have no claim on the originating bank.
example: Say ABC Bank issues $1 billion of covered bonds backed by $1.25 billion of home loans. The overcollateralisation is ($1.25 billion − $1 billion) / $1 billion = 25%, a cushion if some loans default.
formula: Overcollateralisation = (Cover pool value − Covered bonds outstanding) / Covered bonds outstanding

short: A measure of how much traders expect US Treasury yields to swing over the next month, taken from option prices; the bond market's fear gauge.
kid: Imagine asking friends how bumpy they think tomorrow's bus ride will be. The more of them who say very bumpy, the higher the number.
detail: The ICE BofA MOVE Index, created by Harley Bassman at Merrill Lynch in the late 1980s, measures implied volatility in the US Treasury market. It is a weighted average of the implied volatility of one-month options on 2-, 5-, 10- and 30-year Treasuries, expressed in basis points of yield a year. Often called the bond market's VIX, it rises when investors fear sharp moves in rates, as in the 2008 financial crisis or the March 2023 US regional bank turmoil, and falls in calm periods. Because Treasury yields anchor borrowing costs worldwide, a high MOVE reading can tighten financial conditions, hit risky assets and push foreign investors to pull money from emerging markets, including India. Common confusion: the MOVE index does not show the direction of yields, only the expected size of moves in either direction.
example: A MOVE reading of 100 means options are pricing a one-standard-deviation move in Treasury yields of about 100 basis points over a year. Over one month that is roughly 100 / √12 ≈ 29 basis points.
formula: Expected one-month yield move (bps) ≈ MOVE / √12

short: The amount by which a bond auction's highest accepted yield exceeds the market yield just before bidding closed, a sign of weak demand.
kid: Everyone expected the last cupcake to fetch five coins, but the seller had to take four to sell it. The sale went worse than hoped.
detail: In US Treasury auctions, the tail is the gap between the high yield, the highest yield accepted, and the when-issued yield trading just before the bidding deadline. A positive tail means the Treasury had to accept higher yields than the market expected to sell the full amount, signalling weak demand; the opposite, called stopping through, signals strong demand. Traders read tails alongside the bid-to-cover ratio and the share left to primary dealers, who absorb what others do not want. A large tail at a 10- or 30-year auction can push yields higher across the curve. In multiple-price auctions, including many RBI auctions, 'tail' can also mean the gap between the cut-off yield and the weighted average yield, and Indian traders compare the cut-off with pre-auction market yields. Common confusion: a tail is measured in basis points of yield, not money, and a small tail is normal.
example: Say the 10-year note trades at a when-issued yield of 4.250% just before the bidding deadline, and the auction's high yield comes in at 4.275%. The auction tailed by 4.275% − 4.250% = 0.025%, or 2.5 basis points.
formula: Tail = Auction high yield − When-issued yield at the bidding deadline
